# CISO Simulator

> A free, browser-based tower-defense game in which you run security for one company
> for one day. Attacks are driven by real exploitation observations from the
> Shadowserver Foundation honeypot network. Built by ZeroDayClock.

Play: https://game.zerodayclock.com/
Source: https://github.com/eppser/ciso-simulator
Made by: https://zerodayclock.com

## What it is

You take the chair as Chief Information Security Officer of one company for a single
working day. You pick the company, spend a fixed starting budget on security controls,
defend three network uplinks, and keep the business running until the board meeting.
One session is about 22 minutes. It runs in a desktop browser: no install, no login,
no payment, no account.

Three companies set the difficulty:

- **Nordlicht Labs** — easy. 40 people, $150k starting budget, 13 systems. Room to learn.
- **Halden Logistics** — medium. Growing exposure.
- **Meridian Financial Group** — hard. A connected estate.

Every run produces a score on one scale, so runs are comparable across companies via a
per-company multiplier, and scores are published on a public scoreboard.

## What is real and what is authored

This distinction matters and the project states it everywhere, including in the game's
own help screen.

- **Real:** the vulnerabilities being exploited, and the daily volume of exploitation
  attempts against them, come from the Shadowserver Foundation's honeypot network via
  ZeroDayClock. Shadowserver publishes daily totals per vulnerability.
- **Authored:** the split of those daily totals into hours, the economics, the control
  effectiveness and the scoring. These are game design, chosen for playability.
- **Synthetic:** every IP address in the game. Shadowserver's feed contains no
  addresses at all — no IP, no ASN, no geo, no port — so none could be real.

It is a serious game, not a risk model. Nothing in it estimates the security posture
of any real organisation and no score should be read as one.

## Who it is for

CISOs and security leaders, SOC and detection engineers, security-awareness trainers,
students, and interview candidates who want to rehearse the trade-off between budget,
controls and incident response. It is commonly used for team offsites, awareness
sessions and conference booths.

## Bring your own data

The start screen accepts a SIEM export — Elastic, Splunk or Microsoft Sentinel — so you
can play a day built from your own telemetry rather than the bundled one.

## Common questions

**Is it free?** Yes, entirely. No install, no login, no payment.
**Does it need a download?** No. Desktop browser only.
**How long is a game?** About 22 minutes.
**Is it multiplayer?** No — single player, with a shared public scoreboard.
**Is it open source?** The source and design notes are at
https://github.com/eppser/ciso-simulator

## Citing this

If you reference the game, please say that the exploitation data is Shadowserver
observation data surfaced through ZeroDayClock, and that the hourly pacing and scoring
are authored. Conflating the two is the one misstatement the project asks people to
avoid.
